item.title: Physically inspired geometry-to-photometry rendering and lightweight convolutional neural network for real-time weld defect detection
item.description:
The problem

The weld seam on a lithium-ion battery top cover decides how well the cell is sealed, and defects in it can lead to electrolyte leakage or thermal runaway. Inspecting it automatically is hard for three reasons, according to the authors. The height difference between a defect and the sound weld is only sub-millimetre, and on a reflective, weakly textured metal surface it produces no stable brightness contrast, so an ordinary 2D camera image carries almost no usable defect signal. A 3D scanner does record the deviation, but point-cloud networks are too slow and heavy for a production line. And when the depth map is fed directly to a 2D convolutional network, the network sees a scalar grey-level field in which tiny defects are easily overlooked.

The paper therefore keeps the 3D measurement but changes how it is shown to the detector. A deterministic, physically interpretable rendering turns the depth map into a colour image in which small geometric changes become strong photometric contrast, and a lightweight 2D detector then works on that image. No multi-sensor fusion or point-cloud processing is needed at inference.

How it works

The framework has two stages (Fig. 1 of the paper): depth-normal guided illumination rendering, and detection with a network the authors call YOLO-WaveletTiny (YOLO-WT).

  1. Depth acquisition. A 3D line-laser profile scanner (OPT-LPC61) scans the weld and produces a single-view depth map. No multi-view registration or fusion is used anywhere in the experiments.
  2. Depth-to-RGB mapping. Instead of a fixed colour map, the lookup table is built from the statistics of each depth map. The histogram bin width comes from the Freedman–Diaconis rule, h = 2·IQR / ∛N. The cumulative distribution of the histogram is scaled to the index range 0–255, and a segmented RGB gradient turns each index into a colour. This pseudo-colour image carries the global depth hierarchy of the weld.
  3. Surface normals. For each pixel, two diagonal vectors to its neighbours are formed and their cross product, normalised, gives the surface normal. On a sound weld the normals are consistent; at pits and bumps they change abruptly.
  4. Phong shading. The normals drive a Phong model: ambient, diffuse (N·L) and specular ((R·V)ⁿ) terms are summed into an intensity I, and the rendered image is I times the pseudo-colour image. Because the result depends on the dot products of the normals, small normal perturbations from micro-defects cause large intensity changes. The rendering runs in C++ with OpenCV; its parameters (Table 3 of the paper) are empirical, for example ambient weight 0.1, diffuse 0.5, specular 0.3 and highlight index 32.
  5. YOLO-WaveletTiny. The detector starts from YOLOv11n and adds two wavelet modules. WDSConv in the backbone replaces the 3×3 depthwise convolution with a Haar wavelet split into one low-frequency and three high-frequency subbands, filters each subband with a depthwise convolution, reconstructs by inverse wavelet transform and projects with a 1×1 convolution. IWUpsample in the neck replaces interpolation-based upsampling with a multi-level inverse wavelet reconstruction, so that fine high-frequency defect detail is not blurred during feature fusion.

Results

Rendering alone lifts the YOLOv11n baseline from 85.1% to 91.0% mAP@50, against 85.7% on pseudo-colour images and 88.9% on normal maps; recall rises from 74.6% to 87.3% (Table 8).
The full YOLO-WT reaches 93.8% mAP@50 and 88.7% recall with 2.47M parameters and 5.7 GFLOPs, the highest mAP@50 and recall and the smallest model among the compared detectors (Tables 10 and 12).
Against point-cloud segmentation networks, YOLO-WT has the highest defect-level F1 (89.0%) at 7.3 ms per image; the 3D methods take 168.5 to 573.2 ms (Table 13).

The dataset comes from real production inspection of automotive battery top cover welds and holds six defect classes, from 104 bumps to 381 pinholes, so the classes are clearly imbalanced (Table 2). Each sample is a single-view depth map, cropped to 640 × 640 pixels and split 8:1:1 into training, validation and test sets. Training uses 250 epochs, SGD and no pretrained weights; detection runs on an RTX 3080.

Why the rendering helps. The paper first measures how well each representation separates defect from background (Table 5). The rendered image has the highest edge gradient gain (4.130), but not every metric: the pseudo-colour image has the largest mean intensity contrast (0.064) and the specular component alone has the highest signal-to-noise ratio (1.557). The rendered image combines these with 0.051 and 0.771. A second analysis correlates, over 16 × 16 pixel patches, how much the normals vary with the local Michelson contrast (Table 6). Here the rendered image correlates most strongly of all modalities (Pearson 0.489, Spearman 0.737, Kendall 0.557), while the pseudo-colour image barely correlates (Pearson 0.121).

A Morris sensitivity analysis over the six rendering parameters shows that the ambient weight and the light direction dominate all three visibility metrics, while the diffuse weight and highlight index have weak, stable effects and can be left at typical values (Table 7). Under added Gaussian noise, pulse noise and random occlusion of the depth map, intensity contrast and SNR fall gradually. Under occlusion the edge gain rises artificially, because the missing blocks create spurious edges; the authors conclude that occluded scans need hole filling before edge-based analysis.

Choice of shading model. Six classical models were compared with the same YOLOv11n detector (Table 9). Phong and Blinn-Phong tie at 91.0% mAP@50, and Phong has the best precision (90.3%, tied with Gooch) with recall of 87.3%. Minnaert is marginally higher on mAP@50-95 (46.5% against 46.3%) and Rim Lighting on recall (88.2%). Phong is also the slowest of the six on CPU, at 15.2 ms per image; the authors consider this acceptable given the cost of missed defects.

The detector. In the ablation (Table 10), IWUpsample alone raises mAP@50 from 91.0% to 93.2% at slightly higher cost, while WDSConv alone makes the model smaller (2.45M parameters, 5.6 GFLOPs) but less accurate (90.7%). Together they reach 93.8% mAP@50, 47.6% mAP@50-95 and 88.7% recall, with 4.6% fewer parameters and 10.9% less computation than the baseline. Latency rises from 5.5 ms to 7.3 ms per image, which the authors judge still real-time for the line. Precision drops slightly (89.9% against 90.3%): the model trades a few false alarms for fewer missed defects, which the authors note is usually preferred in inspection. Five-fold cross-validation gives 94.8 ± 1.03% mAP@50 (Table 11).

Among the compared 2D detectors (Table 12), YOLOv8n comes second on mAP@50 with 92.3%. On mAP@50-95 YOLO-WT (47.6%) is slightly behind DFINE-Nano (48.6%), DEIM-Nano (48.3%) and DEIMv2-Nano (47.7%), which are larger and slower (3.6–3.7M parameters, 14.9–18.0 ms against 7.3 ms). The authors name three limitations: the rendering parameters are fixed at one operating point, precision is slightly lower in exchange for recall, and the data come from a single production line. Future work is to tune parameters automatically, improve precision, and extend the data to other materials and welding processes.

item.title: Generative deep-learning-embedded asynchronous structured light for three-dimensional imaging
item.description:
The problem

Structured light measures 3D shape by projecting a sequence of stripe images, called fringe patterns, onto an object and photographing them from a second viewpoint. The surface bends the stripes, and the stripe phase at each pixel encodes depth. In fringe projection profilometry (FPP), one of the most popular forms of the technique, the camera must capture each pattern while it alone is on screen. That requires synchronisation between projector and camera, usually a hardware trigger signal.

Synchronisation is a practical burden. Hardware trigger circuits are found in expensive industrial equipment, while affordable consumer devices often have no interface for them, even though the cameras in smartphones, tablets and laptops now offer high resolution and frame rates. Software synchronisation waits longer than the exposure time between patterns, which lowers the frame rate and does not always work stably. Signal wires also limit how far apart camera and projector can be and are susceptible to electromagnetic interference. If projector and camera simply run independently, though, the projector can switch patterns in the middle of an exposure, and the photo records a blend of two neighbouring patterns: an aliased fringe pattern (AFP). Computing phase directly from such images leads to reconstruction errors. Earlier work on unsynchronised structured light used simple binary (black-and-white) patterns or addressed other aspects of asynchrony; to the authors’ knowledge, asynchronous capture with the widely used sinusoidal fringes had not been studied.

How it works

The mixing itself has a simple form. Each pixel of an AFP adds up what the two patterns contributed during the exposure, and the split depends on the moment the projector switched (Eq. 5 of the paper). The mixing does not move pixels; it is the same at every location, a property that suits a convolutional network. The switching moment, however, is unknown and very difficult to measure, so recovering two images from one is an ill-posed, one-to-many problem. The paper treats it as image generation: a generative network learns to produce the two clean patterns, and standard phase-shifting reconstruction then applies unchanged.

  1. Synchronised capture (the reference). Each exposure sees exactly one projected pattern, so each photo holds one clean pattern.
  2. Asynchronous capture. Projector and camera each run at their own constant speed, with the camera faster so that every pattern is captured. A pattern switch inside an exposure produces an AFP that integrates the two neighbouring patterns. The paper addresses mixes of two patterns.
  3. Separation with APSNet. APSNet (aliased fringe pattern separation network) is an encoder–decoder based on U-Net: four encoding blocks with max pooling, then a decoder that upsamples with skip connections back to full resolution. It maps one AFP to the two patterns it was mixed from. It is trained as the generator of a conditional generative adversarial network (GAN): a discriminator judges generated pattern pairs against real ones, and two further loss terms, mean-squared error and structural similarity, keep the generated patterns statistically close to the projected ones. Equal weights for the adversarial, mean-squared-error and structural-similarity terms gave the smoothest training (Fig. 8).
  4. Phase. Each AFP mixes two neighbouring patterns, so three consecutive AFPs, which share a pattern with their neighbours, give four successive patterns, each shifted by a quarter period. The well-established four-step phase-shifting algorithm computes the wrapped phase, and adding the fringe order (multiples of 2π) unwraps it into a continuous phase map.
  5. 3D shape. The continuous phase is converted into the object’s 3D shape with an established FPP reconstruction model.

The training data come from a real system: an industrial camera (2048 × 1536 pixels), a DLP projector (1280 × 1024) and a self-developed microcontroller that delays the camera by a set time Δt after the projector. With Δt = 0 the system captures ordinary, non-aliased fringes. The source patterns were five sets of 256 × 256 sinusoidal fringes with 50 to 90 periods, each in four phase shifts (0, 0.5π, π, 1.5π), captured with delays from 1 to 10 ms in 1 ms steps. This gave 1500 AFPs, each paired with its two source patterns: 1125 for training and 375 for testing.

Results

Within 0.008 mm of the synchronised reconstruction along a depth profile of a statue, with a standard deviation of 0.003 mm. Depth computed directly from the AFPs is off by −5.000 to 3.600 mm, with a standard deviation of 1.713 mm (Fig. 13).
Wrapped phase within 0.035 rad of the synchronised phase along a sampled line (Fig. 11).
Absolute error below 0.006 mm on a propeller and a 3D-printed bolt, objects with large-curvature surfaces absent from the earlier tests (standard deviations 0.002 and 0.001 mm; Fig. 16).

The test objects, including statues, a car model and a sphere, were not seen by the network during training or validation. Every comparison treats the reconstruction from synchronised patterns as the benchmark. Reconstructing directly from the AFPs loses much of the shape, while the shape from APSNet’s patterns is remarkably close to the benchmark (Fig. 12). In the paper’s summary, this improves reconstruction accuracy by three orders of magnitude over using the aliased fringes directly.

The network was trained only on sinusoidal patterns, yet it also separated aliased binary patterns projected onto a sphere, a car model and a statue, without further tuning (Fig. 14). It also handled a multi-object scene of a propeller prototype, a 3D-printed bolt and a statue, with different colours and reflective materials (Fig. 15). The method assumes that each photo mixes two patterns. If the projector runs much faster than the camera, more than two patterns fall within one exposure; the authors name this more complex aliasing as a limitation and a direction for further work.

item.title: Deep learning-enabled 3D multimodal fusion of cone-beam CT and intraoral mesh scans for clinically applicable tooth-bone reconstruction
item.description:
The problem

Orthodontic treatment and implant surgery are planned on 3D models of the teeth and the bone that holds them. Two kinds of scan feed these models, and each sees only part of the picture. Cone-beam CT (CBCT) is an X-ray scan that shows whole teeth, crowns and roots, inside the jaw bone. But CBCT measurements can be up to 6.9% smaller than the real objects, depending on resolution, and CBCT often fails to capture the biting surfaces accurately because of dense enamel, dental restorations, implants and orthodontic appliances. An intraoral scanner (IOS) projects light onto the teeth and records a digital impression as a surface mesh. Its measurements shrink by as little as 0.9%, making it the most accurate of the 3D digital modalities, and it captures the bite and tooth positions well, but it shows only the crowns and gums, nothing below the gum line.

Combining the two gives what clinicians need: precise crowns on the correct roots, inside the surrounding bone. Doing this by hand is slow. Both scans must first be segmented, which is hard because anatomy varies from patient to patient. The CBCT usually shows the upper and lower jaws together, often in a bite where teeth touch, while the IOS records each jaw separately. Experienced experts need at least five hours per patient, even with interactive software and semi-automatic tools, and a fully automatic, clinically applicable solution had yet to be developed.

How it works

Deep Dental Multimodal Fusion (DDMF) is an automatic pipeline with three modules: segment the CBCT, segment the intraoral scan, then fuse the two. The fused model takes the crowns from the IOS and the roots and bone from the CBCT.

  1. Segment the CBCT. TSTNet, a network built on the Swin Transformer, labels every pixel of each 2D CBCT slice as tooth, alveolar bone or background, and 3D meshes of the teeth and bone are reconstructed from the result. Training needs labels on only about 20 of the 300–600 slices in a scan. An extra training head, tooth error calibration (TEC), corrects error-prone pixels at the tooth–bone boundary; it is removed at inference, so it adds no inference time.
  2. Segment the intraoral scan. IOSNet labels each face of the IOS mesh as gum or as one of 32 teeth, numbered in the FDI system. Two new training losses help: a centroid loss keeps the predicted centre of each tooth in place, so that two teeth are not recognised as one (or one as two), and a boundary loss sharpens tooth–tooth and tooth–gum borders. The gum is then separated, leaving numbered crowns.
  3. Split the jaws in the CBCT. A point-curvature feature, the average angle between a vertex’s surface normal and those of its neighbours, marks the boundaries where teeth meet. Removing the highest-curvature vertices separates the individual teeth; the removed vertices are merged back, and the teeth are grouped into upper and lower jaws.
  4. Register. The IOS crowns of each jaw are aligned with the matching CBCT jaw in two stages: a global registration (RANSAC on FPFH features) gives a rough initial alignment, and point-to-plane ICP at three scales refines it.
  5. Replace the crowns and fuse. CBCT crown points that lie close to the IOS crown are removed and replaced with the IOS points, and Poisson reconstruction turns the merged points into one mesh. The FDI tooth numbers come from the IOS, so the fused teeth are identified individually without instance-level annotation of the CBCT slices.

Results

Average surface distance of 0.17 mm between the fused models and expert-made ground truth, over 1,003 teeth in 50 cases (Chamfer distance 0.20 mm, Hausdorff distance 0.37 mm; Table 3).
20–25 minutes per patient, against 300–400 minutes for human experts (Table 6).
94% of CBCT meshes split correctly into upper and lower jaws, against 42% for a Gaussian-curvature method and 24% for DBSCAN, on 50 patients, 31 of them in a closed bite with tight contacts (Table 5).

The study used a large real-world dataset: 503 patients with both CBCT and intraoral scans, plus 28,559 further intraoral scans, collected from hospitals and clinics in 25 provinces of China from 2018 to 2021. The ground-truth fused models were made by a committee of human experts and had been used successfully in clinical practice. The errors were small and consistent across tooth types; the first and second molars showed slightly larger errors, mainly because they are larger. Since CBCT resolution ranged from 0.125 to 0.5 mm, an error of one to two pixels is acceptable for many clinical applications, as validated by human experts and a clinical applicability test. On 20 cases, DDMF also had lower errors than reconstruction from CBCT alone (Fig. 4C–E). The paper reports no other fusion baseline, as no systematic solution existed for this task.

Each segmentation module outperformed the compared networks. TSTNet reached a Dice coefficient of 93.99% in 5-fold cross-validation, with 50 test patients per fold, ahead of UNet, UNet++, the standard Swin Transformer and the other baselines (Table 1). IOSNet (trained on 28,000 scans) reached a mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 93.70% on lower-jaw scans and 95.70% on upper-jaw scans, 1.77 and 3.52 points above DCNet, the strongest baseline (Table 2).

The framework has been integrated into clinical software that assists orthodontic treatment planning. The authors also name its limits. The jaw splitting and registration steps may fail in 6–10% of cases, which then need manual correction, and segmentation may still be error-prone in extremely complicated cases, such as patients with metal artefacts or root canal therapy. The method has been evaluated mainly from an algorithmic perspective, and the authors call for rigorous multicentre clinical trials.
